correctness.rationale: For arbitrary finite simple graphs, each nontrivial tree has an indegree-zero source forced to receive at least one unit of money; this forces each isolate to receive at least one unit by global envy. All cyclic components can be oriented to give every participating vertex one edge, and outward tree orientations with unit-paid roots and unit-paid isolates achieve the lower bound. Isolated-edge counts converge to Poisson by their explicit factorial moments, all tree components of order >=3 have vanishing expected count via separate three size regimes, and isolated vertices concentrate in L2 by first/second moments. The claimed scaled distribution, zero probability and expected cost follow rigorously. Standalone brute-force corroboration covers all simple graphs of order <=4, six examples of order 5, and two finite exact expectation comparisons.

value.rationale: A natural sparse random resource market exhibits an unexpectedly discontinuous compensation scale: a Poisson number of nontrivial tree components activates payments to a diverging isolated-agent population. The exact window, Bernoulli-mixture law, and asymptotic mean solve a motivated stochastic reliability question, not arbitrary finite enumeration. The theorem explains how global cash comparisons propagate localized deficits and provides a quantitative design benchmark for subsidy budgeting.
